Three-vessel and three-vessel-and-trachea views

DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

You will be able to

  • Assess the three-vessel view for number, size, alignment and arrangement.
  • Describe the normal three-vessel-and-trachea view: the V, its side, and the trachea.
  • Name the lesions these two views help to detect.
  • Explain how a finding here changes what happens next.

A continuum, not two pictures

The axial appearances of the right outflow tract, the branch pulmonary arteries and the ductal and aortic arches form a continuum of views. What you see varies with the orientation of the transducer and the lie of the fetus.1

Assessment is likely to be more reliable live or on cine-loop than from still images alone.1

The three-vessel view

Assess four things: the number of vessels, their size, their alignment and their arrangement.2

From left to right the vessels are the pulmonary artery, the aorta and the right superior vena cava. The pulmonary artery is the most anterior and the vena cava the most posterior. The diameters decrease from left to right.2

VesselSideFront to backSize
Pulmonary arteryLeftMost anteriorLargest
AortaMiddleMiddleMiddle
Superior vena cavaRightMost posteriorSmallest

The pulmonary artery is usually slightly larger than the ascending aorta in fetal life. The superior vena cava lies to the right of the aorta.3

The three-vessel-and-trachea view

This is a slightly oblique transverse plane, towards the head from the three-vessel view. It shows the main pulmonary artery continuing into the ductus arteriosus, with the transverse aortic arch just to its right.4

The trachea appears as a bright ring around a small fluid-filled space.4

Normally the ductus arteriosus and the aortic arch both run to the left of the trachea and meet at an acute angle, forming a V. The right superior vena cava and the thymus are also seen in this plane.5

The screening checklist asks for two things here: the V-sign, with both arches to the left of the trachea, and ductal and aortic arches of similar size.6

The thymus appears as a relatively dark area between the great vessels and the front of the chest.7

The aortic arch lies slightly nearer the head than the ductal arch, so showing both together may need a small adjustment away from a true axial plane.8

Adding colour

Colour helps to show the V-sign and can highlight reversed flow in the ductus arteriosus or the aortic arch.9

What these views detect

The two views help to detect anomalies of the outflow tracts, the aortic arch and the systemic veins, including a persistent left superior vena cava, and anomalies of the thymus.10

The three-vessel-and-trachea view is particularly useful for abnormalities of the aortic arch such as coarctation, vascular rings and an aberrant right subclavian artery. It is likely to enable detection of coarctation, right aortic arch and double aortic arch.11,12

Complete transposition, tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, common arterial trunk and pulmonary atresia with a ventricular septal defect can have a four-chamber view that looks normal. They are typically abnormal in the three-vessel view.13

CheckNormalQuestion to ask if not
NumberThree vesselsIs there a fourth vessel, or only two?
SizeDecreasing from left to right; arches similar in sizeIs one great artery or one arch much smaller?
Alignment and arrangementPulmonary artery, aorta, vena cava in a line from left-front to right-backIs the order or the line wrong?
Side of the archesBoth left of the trachea, meeting in a VDoes an arch pass to the right of the trachea, or on both sides?

Why a finding here matters

Anomalies found on the three-vessel views can change counselling and management. What follows depends on the anomaly found; none of these follows from every abnormal view. The guideline's examples: testing for 22q11 microdeletion; planning where delivery takes place, as in complete transposition; being ready to give prostaglandin; being ready for airway problems from vascular compression.14

A fetus with a suspected abnormality on screening is a candidate for fetal echocardiography.15

What the fetal echocardiogram adds

These points are from the echocardiography guideline. They describe the specialist examination, not the screen.

In the three-vessel view, abnormalities of vessel number, size, alignment or arrangement should be recorded.16

In the normal three-vessel-and-trachea view the two arches join the descending aorta on the left of the trachea. Colour Doppler should demonstrate patency and direction of flow in both arches.17,18

Aortic and ductal arch sidedness should be documented at every fetal echocardiogram.19

Colour and power Doppler in the three-vessel-and-trachea view can help to identify an aberrant subclavian artery.20

Three-vessel views checklist

  • Three vessels: pulmonary artery, aorta, superior vena cava, from left to right2
  • Sizes decrease from left to right2
  • Vessels in line, pulmonary artery most anterior, vena cava most posterior2
  • Three-vessel-and-trachea view: ductal and aortic arches meet in a V5
  • Both arches to the left of the trachea5,6
  • Arches similar in size6
  • Clip of these views stored1,21
